text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Ross v. Canada (Attorney General),

2013 BCSC 1464

Date: 20130813

Docket:
S10992

Registry: Campbell River

Between:

Scott
Curtis Ross and Pacific Coast Marine Surveying

Plaintiff

And

The
Attorney General of Canada and

The
Attorney General of British Columbia

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice R. Punnett

Reasons for Judgment

(In Chambers)

Scott Curtis Ross:

Not
appearing

Counsel for the Defendants:

A.S.
Sanghera

Place and Date of Hearing:

Campbell
River, B.C.

July
12, 2013

Place and Date of Judgment:

Campbell
River, B.C.

August
13, 2013

[
1
]

On April 24, 2013 the plaintiffs filed a notice
of civil claim against the two named defendants. The defendants apply pursuant
to Rule 9-5 of the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
for an order that the claim
be struck without leave to amend and that all claims against the defendants be
dismissed. Alternatively, if the notice of civil claim is not struck, the
defendants seek a reasonable time in which to file a response after an order is
made respecting this application.

[
2
]

Mr.
Ross represents himself and Pacific Coast Marine Surveying. While not apparent
from the style of cause he has signed on behalf of an entity described as
Pacific Coast Marine Surveying and Repair Consultants Ltd.

[
3
]

Mr.
Ross did not appear. Counsel provided copies of correspondence of May 21,
2013, June 18, 2013 and July 3, 2013, to Mr. Ross at his address for delivery. Counsel
also provided the facsimile transmission confirmation slips indicating they
were received. No reply was received from Mr. Ross and he filed no response to
the application on behalf of either of the plaintiffs. I am satisfied that the
plaintiffs had notice of the application.

[
4
]

Aside
from receipt of the original notice of civil claim counsel advise that neither
defendant has received any other communication from Mr. Ross nor has he made any
filings in the action.

Background

[
5
]

The
pleadings are problematic as they are scattered, unclear and grammatically
difficult to follow. They appear to advance claims in negligence, defamation,
malicious prosecution, conspiracy, false arrest, false imprisonment, perjury
and
Charter
breaches against the named defendants as well as other
entities not capable of being sued and in many instances, unnamed.

[
6
]

The
allegations appear to originate in an incident that occurred on May 10, 2011
involving a rescue tow of a distressed vessel by the plaintiff.

Law

[
7
]

The
burden is on the defendants to establish that it is plain, obvious and beyond
doubt that the pleading must fail for want of a cause of action. If it is
possible that the plaintiff could succeed on the claim as filed or as may be
amended the plaintiff is entitled to pursue the matter to trial (
Hunt v.
Carey Canada Inc.
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
,
[1990] 2 S.C.R. 959
at p. 15)
.

[
8
]

It is
however incumbent on the plaintiff to plead the material facts necessary to
formulate a cause of action and upon which they rely (
Homalco Indian Band v.
British Columbia

(1988),
1998 CanLII 6658 (BC SC)
,
25 C.P.C. (4th) 107
, para.
5
and Rule 3-1(2)(a) of
the
Rules
).

[
9
]

A
motion to strike a pleading proceeds on the assumption that the facts pleaded
are true. The court must, on that basis, decide if the facts disclose a
reasonable cause of action (
R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd
.,
2011 SCC
42
, at para.
23
). While the pleadings do not have to expressly refer to a
particular cause of action, where multiple causes of action are alleged against
multiple defendants a plaintiff must clearly set out which facts relate to
which cause of action and against which defendant (
Stoneman v. Denman Island
Local Trust Committee,

2010 BCSC 636
, para.
27
).

[
10
]

With
these general principles in mind I turn to the notice of civil claim and the
apparent causes of action pleaded. A copy of the notice of civil claim is
appended to these reasons.

Discussion

Allegation of
Negligence

[
11
]

Paragraphs
5, 7, 18 and “K” appear to assert a claim in negligence however the plaintiffs
do not plead a duty of care, nor material facts, to establish the circumstances
in which a duty was owed nor who owed them a duty of care. The required
material facts are absent (
Young v. Borzoni et al
,
2007 BCCA 16
). These
deficiencies lead to a failure to establish a basis for a claim in negligence
against the defendants.

Defamation

[
12
]

Paragraphs
8, 20, 34 and “H” raise the issue of defamation by simply making bald
assertions of defamation. They fail to set out the alleged defamatory words (
Central
Minera Corp.

v
.
Lavarack
,

2001 BCSC 349
at para.
12
;

Rule
3-7(21)).

[
13
]

They
also fail to demonstrate:

a)

the impugned words were defamatory in the sense that they tend to
lower the plaintiffs reputation in the eyes of a reasonable person;

b)

the words in fact refer to the plaintiff; and

c)

the words were published, meaning that they were communicated to at
least one person other than the plaintiff.

Grant

v
.

Torstar Corporation,

2009 SCC
61
, at para.
28

[
14
]

To the
extent that any facts are pleaded respecting defamation they appear to refer to
statements made by unnamed individuals in court proceedings, statements that
are, when made in judicial proceedings as part of those proceedings, protected
by absolute privilege in any event (
Geyer v. Merritt

(1979),
1979 CanLII 682 (BC SC)
,
16 B.C.L.R.
27 (S.C.)
, affirmed
1980 CanLII 384 (BC CA)
,
26 B.C.L.R. 374 (C.A.)
).

Malicious
Prosecution and/or Conspiracy

[
15
]

The
notice of civil claim in paras. 15, 16, 19, 22-25, 29, 31-37 and 40 make claims
for malicious prosecution and/or conspiracy. While it is difficult to
comprehend their context it appears they relate to involvement of the plaintiff
Mr. Ross in a criminal matter and a Federal Court matter.

[
16
]

The
tort of malicious prosecution requires that a plaintiff prove:

a.         they
were prosecuted;

b.         the
prosecution concluded in their favour;

c.         the
absence of reasonable and probable cause; and

d.         the
prosecution was initiated and/or continued for an improper purpose.

Miazga

v
.

Kvello Estate
,
2009 SCC 51
at
paras.
3
, 53-56

[
17
]

A claim
for damages for conspiracy requires that the pleadings set out that there are
several parties and describe their relationship with each other, the alleged
agreement to conspire, the purpose or objects of the alleged conspiracy and the
acts alleged to have been done to further the conspiracy, and finally the
injury and damage occasioned to the plaintiff as a result (
Cement LeFarge v.

B.C. Lightweight Aggregate
,
1983 CanLII 23 (SCC)
,
[1983] 1 S.C.R. 452
;
Alford

v
.
Canada
(Attorney General of)

(1997),
1997 CanLII 868 (BC SC)
,
31 B.C.L.R. (3d) 228 (S.C.)
at para.
38
).

[
18
]

The notice
of civil claim fails to fulfill these requirements.

False Arrest and
False Imprisonment

[
19
]

Paragraphs
5 and 17 of the notice of civil claim refer to false arrest and false
imprisonment but no material facts are pleaded in support. For example, there
are no facts alleged respecting the circumstances of the alleged arrest and
imprisonment.

Alleged
Charter

Breach

[
20
]

Firstly,
no facts are pleaded to support the alleged
Charter
rights violation. The
pleadings merely allege such in paras. 33 and “E”. This is not sufficient (
Vancouver
(City) v. Ward
,
2010 SCC 27
, at para.
4
). Secondly there are no facts that
would support or demonstrate why
Charter
damages would be appropriate.

Perjury

[
21
]

The
plaintiffs’ claim makes allegations of perjury in paras. 22, 25, 28, 36 and “F”.
As witnesses are immune from civil action there is no tort of perjury (
Pearlman
v. Critchley
,
2012 BCSC 1830
, para.
67
;
McDaniel v. McDaniel
,

2009 BCCA 53
).

Conclusion

[
22
]

In
summary, it is plain and obvious that the notice of civil claim discloses no reasonable
causes of action. While it appears to invoke certain causes of action there are
no material facts pleaded to establish the essential elements of those claims. Others
do not form a basis for a claim. The notice of civil claim is not capable of amendment.
As a result it is struck in its entirety pursuant to Rule

9-5(a) given
it discloses no reasonable claims.

[
23
]

I need
not address the second part of the defendant’s application that the pleadings
be struck because they are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious. However,
in the event I am mistaken in striking the notice of civil claim for disclosing
no reasonable causes of action I do so.

Unnecessary, Scandalous,
Frivolous or Vexatious

[
24
]

Rule
9-5(b) provides that pleadings may be struck where they are unnecessary,
scandalous, frivolous or vexatious.

[
25
]

A
frivolous pleading is one without substance, is groundless, fanciful, trifles
with the court or wastes time (
Jerry Rose Jr.

v
.
The
University of British Columbia
,

2008 BCSC 1661
at para
9
,
quoting from
McNutt

v
.
A.G.
Canada et al
,

2004 BCSC 1113
at para.

40
).

[
26
]

A
pleading is vexatious if it does not disclose a claim known to the law or if
does not establish the cause of action alleged (
Citizens for Foreign Aid
Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
,
36 C.P.C. (4th) 266
(B.C.S.C.)

at para.
47
)
.

[
27
]

A
scandalous pleading is so irrelevant it will result in useless expense and will
prejudice the trial of the action by involving the parties in a dispute
separate from the issues (
Citizens
, para. 47).

[
28
]

As will
be clear from these reasons the pleadings are vexatious as they lack material
facts sufficient to form a basis for any of the claims apparently advanced
against the defendants. They are argumentative, full of speculation and
conjecture and fail to address the most basic requirements for pleadings. The notice
of civil claim cannot be cogently responded to.

[
29
]

For
example the pleadings make a myriad of allegations against “others”, apparently
unidentified members of the community, as well as against a paramedic, a host
of unnamed lawyers including prosecutors (notice of civil claim paras. 7-9, 11,
13, 14, 16, 19, 20, 22, 23 and 30). They also make allegations against the
Federal Court of Canada, an entity that is incapable of being sued (
Morier
and Boily v. Rivard,

1985 CanLII 26 (SCC)
,
[1985] 2 S.C.R. 716
, notice of civil claim paras. 16,
31, 32, 33, 36 and 37).

[
30
]

I find
that it is plain and obvious that the allegations are unnecessary, scandalous
and frivolous or vexatious and strike them for those reasons as well.

[
31
]

The
pleadings also suffer from additional defects.

[
32
]

The
pleadings name the Attorney General of Canada as a defendant on the basis that
the “Attorney General of Canada represents the Federal Court of Canada”. The
Federal Court of Canada is not a legal entity that can sue or be sued and no
action lies for acts or omissions of a judge in the performance of his or her
judicial duties.

[
33
]

The
naming of the Attorney General of British Columbia as a defendant is based on
the allegation that the Attorney General of British Columbia is to “ensure that
crown prosecutors act within there [sic] legal scope”. This appears to invoke
the tort of malicious prosecution, the elements of which as noted earlier, have
not been pleaded.

[
34
]

Finally,
there are references to the Royal Canadian Mountain Police as well as to
individual officers. Firstly the proper defendant is the Provincial “Minister
of Justice”. Secondly, such references found at paras. 5, 7, 9-11, 12, 17, 28,
“J” and “K” fail to advance any claims, contain irrelevant commentary and are
not capable of amendment.

[
35
]

For
these reasons the notice of civil claim is struck in its entirety without leave
to amend. The defendants shall have their costs.

“Punnett J.”

LEGAL BASIS

A)        This
proceeding is pursued under the crown liability and proceedings act .This act
provides and facilitates the responsibilities of the actions of the crown and
its employees.

B)        The
Where two or more persons form an intention in common to carry out an unlawful purpose
and to assist each other therein and any one of them, in carrying out the
common purpose, commits an offence, each of them who knew or ought to have known
that the commission of the offence would be a probable consequence of carrying
out the common purpose is a party to that offence. The employees of the crown
did commit an offence where damages as a result are recoverable.

C)        An
